newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Hungary 96 C/A, trade bal get mixed review.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Hungary 96 C/A, trade bal get mixed review.

text.p: Analysts had mixed opinions on Wednesday as Hungary reported a big drop in its annual current account deficit for 1996 but showed a slight increase in the trade deficit for the year.

Some analysts said the results showed that Hungary's tight monetary policy over the last two years was showing results, but others said the C/A deficit was still higher than it should be at this stage of a recovery.

The figures released by the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) showed a January-December 1996 C/A accumulated deficit of $1.678 billion compared to $2.465 billion for 1995 while the trade deficit was slightly larger at $2.645 billion for 1996 compared to $2.436 billion for 1995.

"It's obviously an improvement over the last couple of years and I guess it's a sign of this continued process of external adjustment that we've seen Hungary going through," said Mark Thirlwell, macroeconomic policy analyst at J.P. Morgan in London.

Thirlwell said there had been improvements in the invisibles, particularly from strong inflows from tourism while outflows were weak because of the general decline in real income for most Hungarians over the past two years.
"My only slight reservation is that in the past we've seen some of these boom-bust cycles...but given that we've seen so much adjustment this time I'm actually pretty optimistic," he added.
Anthony Thomas, director of macroeconomic studies for Kleinwort Benson in London, said the results were more worrying.
"At this stage of a recovery you'd really hope to have a much smaller current account deficit," Thomas said.
He said the market had been looking at a possible $1.5 billion C/A deficit for the year and the actual result was "very much at the upper end of market expectations".

Laszlo Batora at Raiffeisen Securities in Budapest said upswings in the month-on-month figures were cause for concern. The NBH reported that the C/A deficit for December 1996 grew to $501 million, up from $53 million in November and almost double the December 1996 figure of $256 million.
"It's totally normal it's seasonal," Batora said.
"But I think it's not a good sign and I think the leaders of Hungarian economic policy -- the finance minister and the National Bank -- should not decrease the crawling peg."
The Hungarian government has said it wants to further reduce the monthly crawling peg devaluator, which now stands at 1.2 percent per month.
Thomas agreed that reducing the crawling peg would only encourage more imports while having a "pretty much minimal effect on inflation".
